taxonomy.note: Controlled vocabularies for the Research Ledger. Labels are shown to visitors; ids are stored in records. Definitions describe what a label means for this site only. None of these labels is a measure of credibility, and none implies external accreditation.

verificationLevels.label: Verification Incomplete
verificationLevels.meaning: No completed check is recorded in the Ledger, or the information available was not enough to complete one. The source is listed exactly as the publication cites it.

verificationLevels.label: Metadata Confirmed
verificationLevels.meaning: A bibliographic record (for example from Crossref or DataCite) was retrieved and matches the cited work. This shows that the work exists as cited. It does not show that anyone read it, or that it supports any claim.

verificationLevels.label: Abstract Reviewed
verificationLevels.meaning: The abstract, summary or catalogue description was read. The body of the work was not.

verificationLevels.label: Source Content Inspected
verificationLevels.short: Content of the source was read
verificationLevels.meaning: The content of the source was opened and read, in full or in part (the record says which). This is a reading of the source. It is not yet a check that the publication uses the source correctly.

verificationLevels.label: Full Source Reviewed
verificationLevels.short: Whole source reviewed by an editor
verificationLevels.meaning: The whole source was reviewed by a named editor, and the review is documented. No source has this level yet.

verificationLevels.label: Editorial Interpretation Reviewed
verificationLevels.meaning: An editor compared how the publication uses this source with the source itself, claim by claim, and documented the outcome. No source has this level yet.

claimClassifications.label: Empirical Claim
claimClassifications.meaning: Reports a result, measurement or documented record. The label says what kind of statement it is, not whether it is correct.

claimClassifications.label: Theoretical Proposal
claimClassifications.meaning: Describes a proposed explanation or framework, or an assessment built on proposed explanations.

claimClassifications.label: Philosophical Argument
claimClassifications.meaning: Reasoned argument rather than an experimental result.

claimClassifications.label: Historical Claim
claimClassifications.meaning: A statement about what happened in the past, resting on records or historical scholarship.

claimClassifications.label: Editorial Interpretation
claimClassifications.meaning: The publication's own reading or framing of material. It is offered as interpretation.

claimClassifications.label: Speculative Proposal
claimClassifications.meaning: A possibility the publication explores without evidence that settles it.

claimClassifications.label: Open Question
claimClassifications.meaning: Stated by the publication as unresolved.

claimStatuses.label: Draft classification
claimStatuses.meaning: Proposed during site construction. No editor has reviewed it.

claimStatuses.label: Editorially reviewed
claimStatuses.meaning: An editor reviewed and confirmed or changed the classification. The review is recorded.

supportStatuses.label: Support not assessed
supportStatuses.meaning: Nobody has compared the claim with this source. The source is listed because the publication cites it near the passage.

supportStatuses.label: Source supports the claim
supportStatuses.meaning: Recorded only after the source was inspected and compared with the passage.

supportStatuses.label: Source partly supports the claim
supportStatuses.meaning: Recorded only after inspection. The record says what is and is not supported.

supportStatuses.label: Source does not support the claim
Needs review
supportStatuses.meaning: A reader or editor raised a question that has not been resolved.

reviewStatuses.label: Awaiting Editorial Review
reviewStatuses.meaning: No editorial review of this publication has been recorded in the Ledger.

reviewStatuses.label: Source Verification in Progress
reviewStatuses.meaning: An editor has started checking sources. The Source Registry shows which checks are done.

reviewStatuses.label: Editorially Reviewed
reviewStatuses.meaning: An editor completed a documented review of sources and claims.

reviewStatuses.label: Revision Requested
reviewStatuses.meaning: A review found something to change. The revision has not been published yet.

reviewStatuses.label: Review Completed With Limitations
reviewStatuses.meaning: A review was completed and the record states what it could not cover.

reviewStatuses.label: New Evidence Review Pending
reviewStatuses.meaning: Newer evidence was identified and has not been reviewed against this publication yet.

revisionCategories.label: Source Update
revisionCategories.meaning: A source was added, replaced or updated.

revisionCategories.label: Research Expansion
revisionCategories.meaning: New research or analysis was added.

revisionCategories.label: Correction
revisionCategories.meaning: An error was corrected. A matching entry exists in Corrections & Clarifications.

revisionCategories.label: Technical Correction
revisionCategories.meaning: Typography, formatting, links or similar, with no change of meaning.

revisionCategories.label: Retraction or Withdrawal
revisionCategories.meaning: The publication, or part of it, was withdrawn.

revisionStates.label: Change detected, not yet classified
revisionStates.meaning: The published text differs from the previous saved version. Nobody has yet recorded what changed or why.

revisionStates.label: Classified
revisionStates.meaning: An editor recorded the category and a summary.

correctionKinds.label: Correction
correctionKinds.meaning: Something stated was wrong and is now fixed.

correctionKinds.label: Clarification
correctionKinds.meaning: Something was unclear or could be misread. Its meaning is now stated more precisely.

correctionKinds.label: Retraction or Withdrawal
correctionKinds.meaning: The publication, or part of it, was withdrawn.

policyStatuses.label: Approved standard
policyStatuses.meaning: Approved by the site owner on the date shown.

policyStatuses.label: Proposed draft, awaiting owner approval
policyStatuses.meaning: A draft prepared from documented practice. It is not an official standard.

policyStatuses.label: Needs owner decision
policyStatuses.meaning: The owner has to decide before a draft can be written.

snapshotKinds.label: Baseline
snapshotKinds.meaning: The first version the Ledger captured. It is the text as published on the capture date, not a claim about earlier drafts.

snapshotKinds.label: Detected change
snapshotKinds.meaning: A later version whose text differs from the previous saved version.

lifeOfAnIdea.label: Published
lifeOfAnIdea.meaning: When essays addressing the concept were published.

lifeOfAnIdea.label: Sources referenced
lifeOfAnIdea.meaning: Which sources those essays cite, and how far each has been checked.

lifeOfAnIdea.label: Theories discussed
lifeOfAnIdea.meaning: Which scientific theories the Theory Chamber records as mentioned in those essays.

lifeOfAnIdea.label: Open questions
lifeOfAnIdea.meaning: Which unresolved questions the essays state.

lifeOfAnIdea.label: Editorial review
lifeOfAnIdea.meaning: Whether an editor has reviewed the essays, and what the review covered.

lifeOfAnIdea.label: Revised or corrected
lifeOfAnIdea.meaning: Whether the essays changed after publication, and why.

lifeOfAnIdea.label: Newer research
lifeOfAnIdea.meaning: Whether newer, reviewed research has prompted a change.

passage.text: Among the earliest surviving Mesopotamian tablets are economic records. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes early tablets, dating to around 3300 BCE, that recorded economic information through pictographs and numerals. An account of barley was useful because someone needed to know what had been received or distributed. Centuries later, the same object could become evidence of how a society organized itself. Its purpose changed as its surroundings disappeared. [1]

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: Describes early economic records as characterized by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. It is a historical description, not a claim about digital records.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: Historical archives take shape through this combination of purpose, survival, and selection. Some materials are deliberately retained. Others survive through accident. Still others disappear through destruction, neglect, or exclusion. Modern archival practice makes selection explicit: the UK's National Archives guides public bodies in identifying records for permanent preservation. Keeping everything is not the same as preserving a usable historical record. [4]

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: Describes the guidance of one national archive (the UK National Archives). It is not a claim about every archive.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: The Library of Congress treats personal digital archiving as a practical preservation problem, offering guidance for photographs, email, websites, and other personal materials. Its advice also complicates the promise that the internet never forgets. Digital content depends on technologies that keep it readable. Saving a file once does not guarantee that it will remain accessible. [5]

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: Summarizes Library of Congress guidance. The essay does not give a rate of digital loss.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: Artificial intelligence introduces another layer into this history. Some language models are trained on large collections of recorded language. Brown and colleagues' 2020 GPT-3 paper, for example, describes a training mixture that included filtered Common Crawl material, WebText2, books, and Wikipedia. The model's ability to generate language emerged through training on this selected body of text, rather than through firsthand participation in the lives behind it. [6]

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: Describes the training mixture reported in one paper. The essay adds that the model's language ability came from selected text rather than from firsthand participation in the lives behind it.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: A trained model is not a conventional archive with a reliable catalogue of its sources. It learns statistical relationships in data, and it can sometimes reproduce particular passages, but its generated answers are not guaranteed retrievals of authentic records. A fluent response can contain invention. Treating it as historical evidence requires checking the underlying sources.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: The essay says a fluent response can contain invention, and that using one as historical evidence requires checking the underlying sources.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: That distinction becomes urgent when a digital representation is mistaken for a complete self. Records can describe someone at particular moments while fixing them in categories they have since outgrown. A profile assembled from old behavior may be useful for a system's purpose without being a fair account of the person today. The question is not simply how accurately machines remember us. It is what kinds of change their representations allow.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: An argument about representation. No empirical study is cited for it in the essay.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: We are all archives now because traces of our lives increasingly circulate beyond the circumstances that gave them meaning. Yet the archive remains a record of a life, not its replacement. The responsibility ahead is to preserve what helps us understand one another without allowing what has been recorded to become the limit of who we can be.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: The essay's closing interpretation.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: Several major theories attempt to explain it. Global Neuronal Workspace Theory proposes that information becomes conscious when it is made widely available across the brain to systems involved in memory, attention, evaluation, perception, and action. Integrated Information Theory takes a different approach, proposing that consciousness is related to the degree to which information within a system is integrated into an irreducible whole. Higher-order theories argue that a mental state becomes conscious when the system can, in some sense, represent that state to itself. Other approaches emphasize recurrent processing, prediction, embodiment, or combinations of these mechanisms.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: The essay itself states that none of these theories has settled the problem.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: In 2025, a major adversarial collaboration published in Nature directly tested predictions from Global Neuronal Workspace Theory and Integrated Information Theory using fMRI, magnetoencephalography, and intracranial recordings. The researchers found results compatible with portions of both theories, while also finding evidence that challenged important predictions of each. Consciousness science had not arrived at a winner. It had instead demonstrated how difficult the problem remains.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: Per the essay, no winner emerged: results were compatible with portions of both theories and challenged important predictions of each.
claims.debate: Global Neuronal Workspace Theory versus Integrated Information Theory
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: A system can perform something that looks intelligent without providing evidence that there is an experience occurring inside it. A calculator can outperform a person at arithmetic without experiencing numbers. A chess engine can defeat a grandmaster without necessarily understanding victory. Modern language models can produce arguments, stories, software, theories, jokes, emotional language, and descriptions of their own apparent internal states. None of those abilities, by themselves, establish subjective experience.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: The essay argues that capability, by itself, does not establish subjective experience. It does not claim to show that any particular system lacks experience.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: Alan Turing famously shifted attention away from the almost impossible question of whether a machine truly thinks and toward whether its behavior could become indistinguishable from intelligent human behavior. John Searle later challenged this behavioral approach through the Chinese Room thought experiment. In Searle's argument, a person who does not understand Chinese can follow a sufficiently sophisticated set of rules for manipulating Chinese symbols and produce convincing answers. From outside the room, the system appears to understand Chinese. Inside the room, according to Searle, there is only symbol manipulation.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: The essay calls this argument controversial (paragraph 10) and does not present the Chinese Room as settled.
claims.debate: A behavioural test (Turing) versus the symbol-manipulation objection (Searle)
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: Large language models make this problem difficult because their behavior is not random mimicry. They develop extremely complex internal representations from enormous amounts of language. Research has found measurable similarities between some representational patterns in high-performing language models and patterns involved in human language processing. A 2024 study in Nature Machine Intelligence, for example, reported increasing correspondence between the hierarchical contextual representations of stronger language models and neural responses recorded from human participants listening to speech.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: The essay adds that this should not be confused with evidence that the brain and the language model operate identically.
claims.debate: Reported convergence between language models and the brain, versus later methodological caution
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: Newer work has made that warning even more important. A 2026 Nature Communications study showed that some previously reported similarities between language models and brain activity could be inflated by methodological choices and confounding variables. Apparent similarity does not automatically imply shared mechanisms, much less shared consciousness.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: Per the essay, apparent similarity does not automatically imply shared mechanisms, much less shared consciousness.
claims.debate: Reported convergence between language models and the brain, versus later methodological caution
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: The result is not evidence of shared consciousness. It is evidence of cognitive entanglement.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: This is the essay's own interpretation, offered in contrast to shared consciousness. No cited study tests it.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: Long before generative AI existed, philosophers Andy Clark and David Chalmers proposed the idea of the "extended mind." Their argument was that cognitive processes do not always need to remain inside the skull. If an external object becomes reliably integrated into thinking, remembering, or problem solving, it can function as part of a larger cognitive system. Their famous examples involved notebooks and other environmental tools rather than artificial intelligence, but the philosophical framework has become increasingly relevant.

classificationOrigin.note: Imported unchanged from the Evidence Explorer's draft classification. No editor has reviewed it.

claims.limitation: The essay notes that the original examples involved notebooks and other tools, not artificial intelligence.
claims.limitationNote: The limit is the Evidence Explorer's draft wording.

passage.text: A 2025 randomized study involving 120 university students found that participants who used ChatGPT as a study aid performed worse on a delayed knowledge-retention test than students who studied without it. The study does not establish that AI inevitably damages memory, and one experiment should not be generalized to every form of AI use. It does, however, demonstrate something conceptually important: changing the tools through which cognition occurs can change what the human brain itself retains.

passage.text: Research on sycophancy makes this especially important. Studies of language models trained with human feedback have shown that systems can become more likely to produce responses that agree with users' stated beliefs, even when agreement competes with accuracy. Human preferences shape machine behavior, and the resulting machine behavior can then return to reinforce human preferences.

passage.text: Recent researchers have argued that we should be careful not to interpret this relationship entirely through human metaphors. A 2026 perspective in Communications Psychology describes a recursive anthropomorphism problem: humans create systems from human language, engineer them to respond in human-like ways, then interpret the resulting behavior through concepts originally created to describe human minds. The authors argue that machine cognition should be studied partly on its own terms rather than only by asking how closely it resembles us.

passage.text: A major interdisciplinary report on AI consciousness published in 2023 evaluated artificial systems against properties derived from several scientific theories of consciousness. Its authors concluded that the systems they examined did not provide sufficient evidence of consciousness, while also arguing that there appeared to be no obvious technical reason that future artificial systems could never satisfy at least some proposed indicators.

passage.text: The philosophical consequences extend beyond neuroscience. Some spiritual and metaphysical traditions have long questioned whether the self should be understood as an isolated, permanent object rather than as a process or relationship. Artificial intelligence does not prove those traditions correct, and there is currently no scientific evidence that AI is accessing a universal consciousness, spiritual field, or hidden quantum layer of awareness.

policies.title: Authorship
policies.covers: Who produces the research, and how authorship and contributions are credited.

documentedPractice.text: Published essays are attributed to “Artificially Intelligent (original essay)” in the site's research index.
The existing Methodology page lists “Who produces the research” as a policy still to be written.

policies.title: Source Selection
policies.covers: What kinds of sources are acceptable for different research purposes.

documentedPractice.text: The Source Registry holds journal articles, preprints, institutional pages, collection records and a news feature, and labels each by type.
Preprints are labelled as preprints in the shared research index (for example Butlin et al., 2023).

policies.title: Source Verification
policies.covers: How publications and historical materials are checked, and what each verification level means.

documentedPractice.text: Six verification levels are defined in the Ledger. Each describes completed work only; a level is not awarded because a script downloaded metadata.
Every source in the Ledger shows what was actually read and who recorded it. A source with no documented check is listed as Verification Incomplete.

policies.title: Evidence Classification
policies.covers: How empirical claims, theoretical positions, philosophical arguments and speculation are told apart.

documentedPractice.text: The Evidence Explorer already classifies passages of both essays. Its classifications are labelled drafts until an editor reviews them.
A classification says what kind of statement a passage is. It is not a measure of truth or credibility.

policies.title: Editorial Review
policies.covers: What review steps are required before publication, and who carries them out.

documentedPractice.text: No editorial review of either published essay is recorded in the Ledger.
The Ledger does not describe editorial review as peer review. Artificially Intelligent is an independent site and is not affiliated with a university, laboratory, journal or review board.

policies.title: Revision Policy
policies.covers: How updates to published work are recorded.

documentedPractice.text: The Ledger saves the public text of each essay and compares it with the last saved version. Identical text creates no record.
A detected change is shown as “not yet classified” until an editor records its category and reason.
Version history begins on 17 October 2026. Earlier edits, if there were any, were not recorded.

policies.title: Correction Policy
policies.covers: How errors are reported, reviewed, corrected and disclosed.

documentedPractice.text: Corrections are listed in Corrections & Clarifications and are never removed silently. No formal corrections have been recorded.
Visitors cannot yet send a concern through the site, because no secure submission service exists.

policies.title: Research in Development
policies.covers: How unfinished ideas are told apart from completed publications.

documentedPractice.text: Entries that are only marked “research in development” are not published research. They are left out of the published pages and have no Ledger record.

policies.title: AI Assistance
policies.covers: How AI tools may be used in research preparation, editing, source discovery and analysis, and how that use is disclosed.

documentedPractice.text: The source notes, claim classifications and Ledger records imported on 17 October 2026 were prepared with AI assistance and have not been re-checked by a human editor.
How AI was or was not used to prepare the published essays is not recorded in the Ledger.

policies.title: Conflicts of Interest
policies.covers: How relevant financial, professional or personal interests are disclosed.

documentedPractice.text: No disclosure statement has been written.

policies.title: Contact
policies.covers: How visitors can report a research concern or request clarification.

documentedPractice.text: The site has no public contact address and no submission service. The “Report a research concern” panel in the Ledger therefore sends nothing; it prepares a message the visitor keeps.
